practice_questions.text:
Which research method did Willis use in his 1977 study 'Learning to Labour'?
A) Structured questionnaire
B) Analysis of official statistics
C) Participant observation
D) Structured interviews only
Define the term 'triangulation' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that triangulation involves using more than one research method; 1 mark for explaining that the purpose is to cross-check or compare findings to increase confidence in conclusions. Example: 'Triangulation is the use of more than one research method in a single study, so that findings from one method can be checked against findings from another, increasing confidence in the conclusions. For example, Halsey combined survey data with interviews in his Origins and Destinations research.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one practical problem sociologists face when conducting research in schools.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a valid practical issue (access through gatekeepers / researcher influence / time and cost / obtaining parental consent); 2 marks for a developed description applying the issue specifically to educational research. Example: 'Gaining access to schools requires permission from several gatekeepers — the headteacher must agree to the research, individual teachers must open their classrooms, and parents must give consent for their children to participate. Each level of gatekeeping can distort the data: a headteacher might only allow observation of their best lessons, meaning the researcher never sees everyday school life. This limits the validity of the findings.'

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of using official statistics to research educational achievement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks for two developed points. Strength: official statistics from the Department for Education are large-scale, covering all state schools in England, and longitudinal — allowing researchers to track attainment trends by class, gender and ethnicity over many years, as Halsey did in Origins and Destinations. This gives high reliability: the same data can be cross-checked and compared by different researchers. Weakness: official statistics are socially constructed — they reflect decisions about what to measure. League tables measure exam results but not the value a school adds to pupils' progress. A school serving a disadvantaged intake may appear less effective than one in a wealthy catchment area, when in reality it may be adding more to its pupils' development.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that participant observation is the best method for researching what happens inside schools.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8-9): Arguments for: participant observation generates high validity — Willis's Learning to Labour is the classic example, revealing counter-school culture through months of direct observation. Arguments against: practical problems — access requires multiple gatekeepers; researcher influence changes classroom behaviour (reducing validity); time-consuming and expensive; findings may lack generalisability (Willis studied twelve boys in one school). Alternative methods: official statistics allow large-scale trend analysis (Halsey); interviews allow focused exploration of specific issues; triangulation (Ball) combines both. A judgement that weighs whether participant observation is 'best' in context or whether the most appropriate method depends on the research question. Named sociologists from the education unit used as examples. Sustained sociological vocabulary. Secure (5-7): Both sides, named examples, judgement present. Developing (3-4): Mostly one-sided, some examples, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-2): Basic description of one method, little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the ethical issues sociologists face when researching the experiences of pupils in schools.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Full range of ethical issues addressed with specific strategies. Informed consent: complex with children because parental consent is also required; this may introduce class bias (only engaged parents respond). Strategy: written consent forms sent home, clear explanation of research aims, right to withdraw stated. Confidentiality: pupils may share sensitive information about labelling, poverty or bullying. Strategy: pseudonyms for schools and individuals (Willis: Hammertown; Ball: Beachside), anonymisation in publications. Harm to participants: sensitive questions about negative school experiences can cause psychological distress. Strategy: sensitive interviewing, debriefing, withdrawal rights. Tension between confidentiality and safeguarding: if a researcher discovers serious harm, the duty to report overrides confidentiality. Judgement that weighs whether ethical issues in school research can be fully resolved or whether they involve ongoing tensions. Comparison and contrast of strategies is explicit. Secure (7-9): All three ethical issues addressed with strategies, judgement present. Developing (4-6): One or two issues described with strategies, one-sided, assertive conclusion. Emerging (1-3): Basic list of issues, no strategies, little evaluation.
